items.claim: A campaign describes its own supporters as "concerned citizens" and its opponents' identical activity as "agitators bussed in from outside".
items.explanation: The same behaviour receives opposite labels. There is an attribution asymmetry underneath, which makes that a defensible second choice — but what is being asked about is the vocabulary doing the work, and the question is which lever is being pulled on the reader.

items.claim: "The report says the risk is not significant. So there is no meaningful risk to residents."
items.explanation: "Significant" moves from its statistical sense to its everyday one between the two sentences. A statistically non-significant result can describe a large and worrying effect measured imprecisely — the terms are not interchangeable, which is exactly what the argument relies on.

items.claim: "In a 10-minute televised debate, a candidate unleashes 47 distinct, rapid-fire half-truths and fabricated statistics, making real-time refutation impossible in the remaining time."
items.explanation: Overwhelming an opponent with an excessive volume of specious arguments that take far longer to disprove than to utter.

items.claim: A profile explains a founder's success entirely through her discipline and vision, mentioning in passing that the family funded the first two years.
items.explanation: Traits are credited with an outcome that had substantial situational support. Survivorship bias is the tempting alternative and would apply to a claim about founders in general; this is about the causal account of one case.

items.claim: A small false claim is circulating in one niche forum. An agency issues a national press release naming and rebutting it.
options: The countermeasure amplifies what it targets
items.explanation: The rebuttal carries the claim to an audience that had never encountered it, and repetition increases familiarity, which increases believability. Proportionality is the whole skill — the right response to a contained claim is often containment.

items.claim: An image carries a C2PA manifest that parses cleanly. The viewer shows the capture device, edit history and signer.
options: The manifest is parsed but not cryptographically verified
The manifest proves the device model
items.explanation: Parsing reads what a file claims about itself; verification requires checking the COSE signature against a trusted certificate chain and confirming the asset hashes still match. A well-formed manifest can be copied wholesale onto a different image.

items.claim: A trader keeps a journal of every prediction that came true and remembers the losing calls as "the market being irrational that week".
items.explanation: The record and the memory are curated after the fact. Hindsight bias is the neighbour — that would be misremembering how confident he WAS beforehand, whereas here the question is which events he retains at all.

items.claim: "Inspecting a crowd photograph reveals that distant spectators' earlobes blend seamlessly into their collars, and glasses frames fade into cheek skin without hinges."
items.explanation: Generative diffusion models struggle with fine semantic topological continuity around complex accessory boundaries.

items.claim: Four hundred accounts supporting a zoning proposal were created within the same eleven-day window last year, and share a posting-time distribution unlike the platform baseline.
items.explanation: Creation-date clustering plus an anomalous activity rhythm is coordination evidence, which is what separates this from bandwagon — bandwagon is a fallacy about crowd size being offered as a reason, astroturfing is a claim that the crowd is manufactured.

items.claim: A team reviewing a failed launch reads the pre-launch risk memo and finds that it "obviously flagged the problem", though at the time nobody acted on it.
items.explanation: Knowing the outcome makes the warning legible in a way it was not beforehand. This is why post-incident reviews asking "who missed this" produce worse findings than ones asking "what was visible at the time".

items.claim: "Since the city started spraying organic mosquito repellent in July, local bakery sales have doubled. Clearly, mosquito repellent stimulates carbohydrate appetite."
items.explanation: Confuses chronological sequence with causal relationship ('after this, therefore because of this').

items.claim: "If it is raining, the street is wet. The street is wet. Therefore, it is raining."
items.explanation: A formal deductive error: the street could be wet from a fire hydrant, street sweeper, or melting snow.

items.claim: A segment on a well-replicated finding gives equal airtime to the one researcher who disputes it and to the consensus position, without saying how many hold each.
items.explanation: Equal time misrepresents the state of the evidence as an even split. Manufactured doubt is the strategy this often serves, but that names a deliberate campaign; false balance is the editorial artefact, which frequently occurs without one.

items.claim: A menu lists a $180 tasting option at the top. Sales of the $95 option rise sharply, although it did not change.
items.explanation: The expensive item may sell rarely and still earn its place by re-scaling every other price. Nothing about the $95 dish changed — only the reference point it is judged against.

items.claim: Personas are built with two years of backdated ordinary posts — recipes, sport, holiday photographs — before ever mentioning politics.
items.explanation: Legend-building is asset preparation; the mundane history exists to defeat exactly the account-age and content-mix checks a reviewer would run. It becomes a deployed astroturf campaign only once those assets are used to simulate a movement.

items.claim: A local paper runs six stories in a month about assaults in one park. Reported crime there does not change, but residents petition to close it.
items.explanation: The frequency of COVERAGE changed, not the frequency of events, and the two are being read as one signal. Note that this requires no bad actor at all — ordinary editorial choices produce it.

items.claim: "Four million subscribers cannot be wrong about this trading strategy."
items.explanation: Headcount is offered as proof. Astroturfing is the distractor worth pausing on: that would require the crowd to be MANUFACTURED, and nothing here suggests the subscribers are inauthentic — only that their number is irrelevant to whether the strategy works.

items.claim: A fabricated claim is posted first to a small niche forum, then screenshotted into a mid-size channel as "people are saying", then covered by a national outlet as a controversy.
options: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution
items.explanation: Each hop strips provenance and adds apparent credibility until the origin is unrecoverable. Flooding is a different mechanism — volume rather than laundering — and the tell here is the deliberate ladder of venues.

items.claim: "When confronted about human rights abuses in prison facilities, the minister replies: 'What about your country's mass surveillance programs in 2013?'"
items.explanation: Deflects criticism by raising a counter-accusation of hypocrisy without addressing the underlying offense.
